CONGRANT.TITLE: Equipment: MRI: Track 1 Acquisition of Polytec MSA-600 Micro System Analyzer for Biomedical Engineering
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Requested Instrument: Polytec MSA-600-X/U Micro System Analyzer ($695,790), state-of-the-art instrument crucial for biomedical engineering research and education the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV). The location of the instrument is the BIO-MEMS Laboratory (Director Caruntu). Servingover 34,000 students, UTRGV is a non-PhD-granting, minority-serving institution with a predominantly Hispanic student body (92%). The university aims to become an emerging research institution and establish a strong biomedical engineering community. This advanced equipment is crucial to preparing students in engineering, science, and medicine by providing hands-on research experiences that can lead to graduate studies, academic roles, or leadership positions in industry. UTRGV is experiencing rapid growth, with increasing student enrollment and the hiring of new faculty. A recently formed Biomedical Engineering(BME) Cluster for research and education includes eight faculty members, four of whom were hired within the past two years. Supporting faculty research development depends on access to cutting-edge infrastructure like the requested analyzer. Securing this grant lays a foundation for attracting external funding and fostering multidisciplinary collaborations. The lack of this instrument currently limits research efforts. This proposal is strongly supported by UTRGV administration, aligning with the university’s strategic goal of building a robust biomedical engineering research and education program.

CONTENT_GOAL: GOAL 17: Partnerships to achieve the Goal
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The RESCUE (Renewable Energy for Sustainable, Continuous, Uninterrupted Ecosystems) project proposed by The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) addresses the critical issue of energy insecurity in the underserved and economically disadvantaged communities in the region by developing a Hybrid Energy Systems Testbed to serve as a foundational platform for: (1) Applied R&D in energy systems, (2) Workforce training in related technology areas, and (3) Community demonstration of diverse energy platforms for impact and cost efficiency.The Rio Grande Valley (RGV) experiences some of the state’s most severe and frequent power outages, compounded by a regional poverty rate exceeding 24%, which prevents households and small businesses from investing in backup energy systems. RESCUE directly responds to this challenge by establishing a functioning testbed at UTRGV’s Advanced Manufacturing Research Facility (AMRF) that integrates solar, wind, and battery energy storage into a unified hybrid system. This testbed will serve as the foundation for future applied research, scalable workforce training programs, and visible demonstrations of community-relevant energy solutions.

CONGRANT.TITLE: CREST Center for Multidisciplinary Research Excellence in Cyber-Physical Infrastructure Systems (MECIS)
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Overview:
The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) proposes to establish the “CREST Center for Multidisciplinary Research Excellence in Cyber-Physical Infrastructure Systems (MECIS).” The Center’s mission is to advance and transform the much-needed research and education at the nexus of automation, sensors, and artificial intelligence (AI), as integral parts of the “NSF’s 10 Big Ideas,” anticipating the revolutionary cyber-physical infrastructure systems (CIS). Three Colleges of Engineering, Sciences, and Education at UTRGV in collaboration with the Universities of Illinois (at Urbana-Champaign and at Chicago) and California (Riverside) will pursue multidisciplinary research on CIS, aiming to: (i) transfer technology to various transportation, logistics, manufacturing, and construction industries; and (ii) prepare a minority STEM workforce to drive future CIS-based communities. The Center envisions a portfolio of three research subprojects on automation, sensors, and AI that bridges diverse STEM disciplines. A holistic, multi-level approach is adopted to address CIS planning, design, and operation. While each subproject constitutes a unique element, their synergy ensures the CIS integrity.
Subproject 1 pushes the frontiers of knowledge in future transportation infrastructure, which will be transformed by autonomous vehicles (AVs) and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), in six directions: (i) at the planning level, public acceptance and policy issues of (U)AV; (ii-iv) at the design level, computer vision, automatic navigation, and model/field-based testing of the designed capabilities; and (v, vi) at the operation level, human-(U)AV interactions and network-wide inter-(U)AV interactions.
Subproject 2 designs and embeds sensors in CIS for two purposes. First, (U)AV sensors help perform automated tasks. Second, sensors in civil infrastructure and (U)AVs monitor infrastructure health. Three research areas are defined: (i, ii) at the design level, computational simulation, synthesis, and 3D printing of sensor materials and UAV structures, and (iii) at the operation level, cost-effective decision-making to upkeep infrastructure health using sensor data.
Since (U)AVs and sensors will inherently generate big data, Subproject 3 will synchronously work with subprojects 1 and 2 to: (i) develop AI solutions for big data management, and (ii) develop AI algorithms for big data analytics and decision making in the design and operation of (U)AVs and infrastructure.
UTRGV is the nation’s second largest Hispanic-Serving Institute (HIS) located in South Texas with an established record of preparing underrepresented minority students for STEM careers. The Center will provide (under)graduate students with cutting-edge CIS research experience, will integrate CIS research and education, and will pave a pathway from High School through graduate programs in STEM disciplines. This broad initiative at UTRGV will also offer new courses related to the subprojects. The Center will further enhance the research infrastructure at UTRGV and will strengthen the research competitiveness of a diverse group of faculty.
Intellectual Merit:
The proposed self-sustaining Center will play a key role in transforming the scientific discoveries at the intersection of automation, sensors, and AI technologies, which are the integral elements of next-generation CIS. The Center will address current gaps in the planning, design, and operation of CIS by proposing innovative theoretical, computational, experimental, and empirical solutions spanning from micro (molecule)- to macro (system)-scale, which also yield practical solutions valuable for the industry.
Broader Impacts:
The Center’s research and education activities will develop an underrepresented workforce equipped with the skills to address complex societal problems. The Center will partner with the public and private sectors to advance technology transfer and product development in CIS. The Center’s activities are key for the establishment of an inaugural engineering doctoral program, which will be vital in elevating UTRGV to a Research I institution and advancing the CIS research agenda in a predominantly HSI. The Center's research findings will be made available to the research community as journal publications and conference proceedings, which will inform other domains undergoing related transformations, such as the health industry, manufacturing and production systems, and the military.

CONGRANT.TITLE: NIH SEPA: Biomedical @ the Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The SEPA Biomedical @ the Rio Grande Valley Project will take multi-faceted approach to research educational interventions with the ultimate goal of broadening biomedical research participation of underrepresented Hispanic students from the Lower Rio Grande Valley of Texas on the U.S./Mexican Border. This region of Texas has the highest poverty rate in the United States and a population that is over 90% Hispanic. Most high school teachers are not prepared to teach biomedical curriculum nor the training and skills to carry out biomedical research. As a result, students are not exposed to biomedical research experiences that would help them to be prepared for pursuing a STEM or STEM related undergraduate degree. This problem is <u>magnified</u> for underrepresented populations who lack access to high quality, equitable education opportunities. This proposal seeks to address this problem by (1) providing summer research experiences for high school teachers. High school teachers will gain biomedical research content and knowledge through these paid summer research experiences. (Sub Aim 1 of Specific Aim 1). Participant high school teachers will also work with UTRGV education faculty to develop biomedical experiential learning modules during their summer internships to incorporate into their high school teaching (Sub Aim 2 of Specific Aim 1) in order to increase biomedical content and skills for high school students. (2) Specific Aim 2 will have under-represented high school students perform biomedical research side-by-side with high school teachers during the summer, implementing an educative learning model to increase biomedical research content, knowledge and enthusiasm for these students. (3) Specific Aim 3 will provide high school students with biomedical experiential learning using a university mobile science laboratory. Hypothesis: mobile laboratory activities will have a positive impact on high school students’ attitudes toward STEM careers. Our short-term goal is to excite students about careers in biomedical science and to strengthen ties between area schools and UTRGV. Our midterm goal is to increase educational attainment in STEM to ultimately increase representation of Hispanics in the biomedical science workforce. Educational research will focus on a large number of at-risk students in the Lower Rio Grande Valley, which will enable ultimately crafting programs that succeed at increasing educational equity for these students and representation in biomedical science careers.

CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The goal of this project is to develop and sustain the DOE Consortium of Advanced Additive Manufacturing Research and Education for Energy Related Systems (DOE CA2REERs) to expose, recruit, engage and train students from underrepresented groups for a career in Advanced Manufacturing for Energy, following a collaborative approach by a team of investigators from 3 MSI institutions and 2 DOE Labs. The minority serving education institutions include: University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (90% Hispanic), University Texas San Antonio (54% Hispanic), and University of Arizona (30% minority). The DOE/NNSA labs are Oak Ridge National Lab and Los Alamos National Lab. The consortium covers minority communities at three minority serving institutions with a total student enrollment of around 100,000 (UTRGV 27,708, UTSA 32,101, and University of Arizona 44,831). The long-term vision of the consortium is to cultivate an innovation driven manufacturing education ecosystem for Energy Innovation with programs designed to recruit young talents and prepare them with solid education and real-life experiences in energy innovation and advanced manufacturing technologies. Upon graduation, students are ready for a dream career in DOE/NNSA labs and energy industries.

CONGRANT.SPONORG: DoD U.S. Army Contracting Command – Aberdeen Proving Ground – Research Triangle Park Division
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Groundbreaking advances in advanced manufacturing processes and smart technologies for cyber-physical systems are driving revolutions in materials/structures design and synthesis, providing innovation opportunities that transform a broader spectrum of military systems where advanced performance and protection at extreme conditions are expected. The objective of this request is to support a stream of ongoing research projects and two national consortia led by the PI team, through which 4 minority institutions are supported. Specifically, this requested major equipment supports UTRGV DoD Consortium for Innovation Driven Research Education for Advanced Manufacturing for the Defense (I-DREAM4D, www.idream4d.org) funded by DoD ($3.9 million, 2020-2024). The consortium is composed of five higher education institution members with three minority-serving institutions (UTRGV, UTSA, and Virginia State University), two national labs (Army Research Lab, Oak Ridge National Lab), members from defense industry, local high schools, and community colleges. The requested metal additive manufacturing machine facilitates the goals of the consortium to 1) advance research in material engineering through additive manufacturing (AM) and AI; 2) sustain an innovation-driven manufacturing education ecosystem to prepare future scientists and engineers who lead U.S. defense manufacturing innovation; and 3) expose and recruit future STEM talents through high school summer manufacturing innovation camps, and regional defense expos/exhibitions planned in 5 regions the consortium serves with a total population of 20 million, most of which are from underrepresented minority groups.
UTRVG, a multi-campus and the nation’s second-largest Hispanic-serving institute (HSI) has a record high total enrollment of 32,618 in Fall 2020, of whom 89.4% are Hispanic. The requested equipment is critical to the goal of increasing participation of underrepresented minorities in all STEM programs and specifically in advanced materials and manufacturing while broadening and enhancing UTRGV’s core priority of student success through engaged learning, research, and creative works that will transform the Rio Grande Valley, the Americas, and beyond.
The requested Metal Additive Manufacturing Equipment supports funded research projects and education programs organized in three levels, with the participation of minority students and faculty at UTRGV: 1) Advanced material synthesis and additive manufacturing science; 2) Materials/structure design enabled by AM and Artificial Intelligence (AI); and 3) Military devices and components enabled by AM and AI. Since 2019, the team has engaged more than 652 undergraduate students in the defense manufacturing education program, supported more than 95 students in funded research and industry projects, and exposed 1300 high school students to advanced defense manufacturing technologies though defense expos, summer camps, and invited talks provided by DoD. The team at UTRGV was recenlty selected by DOE/NNSA and NSF for awards of two large grants ($9 million total) to prepare STEM talents and to advance research at UTRGV, leveraging AM for energy production and critical infrastructures. Currently, the team only has limited access to a Renishaw AM 400 machine located in LA, California, through a collaboration arrangement, which is no longer sufficient to support the research and education programs at UTRGV. The pandemic has additionally caused serious logistic challenges to all operations at every facet. Direct access to modern metal additive manufacturing machines is in desperate need to support a stream of funded projects, support student learning in STEM, and support impactful outreach programs the team offers.

CONGRANT.TITLE: MRI: Acquisition of a Scanning Transmission Electron Microscope (STEM) for Advanced Materials Research and Education Programs at the Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
PROJECT SUMMARY

Overview:
The objective of the present MRI proposal is to acquire a state-of-the-art Scanning Transmission Electron Microscope (STEM) that will support interdisciplinary research and education programs at UTRGV. The STEM combines the principles of transmission electron microscopy and scanning electron microscopy. The proposed instrument (Talos™ F200i) is flexible and compact 200 kV Field Emission Gun (FEG) STEM, designed for precise and quantitative characterization of nanomaterials and biological cells. It combines an outstanding quality in high-resolution STEM imaging with Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS). In addition, the instrument is equipped with tomographic capabilities via software for alignment of a tomographic series of images, and 3D reconstruction of the data.

Intellectual Merit:
The acquisition of the Talos™ F200i STEM instrument will enable a significant enhancement of basic research toolset across a wide range of materials, medical education and research programs including Chemistry, Physics, Medicine and Mechanical, Electrical and Manufacturing Engineering at UTRGV. Specifically, the proposed equipment will support projects to advance the development and characterization of different nanoparticles as lubricant additives, composite nanofibers, high entropy alloys (HEA) prepared by Selective Laser Melting technology, regenerative medicine, polymers, and nanomaterials for use in , patterned magnetic arrays, temperature controlled drug delivery systems, bioimaging, nanostructured energetic devices, semiconductors, high temperature superconductors, and radiation induced functional materials. The acquisition of the STEM will broaden the research scope for all participants, making it possible to address new scientific challenges in new transformative research directions.

Broader Impacts:
This proposal brings together a diverse group of faculty members and will significantly impact UTRGV transition towards an emerging research institution. In addition, most of the projects will be carried out by undergraduate and M.S. students. Specifically, the instrument will strengthen existing courses and several more will be developed as a result of this funding. Additionally, it will significantly support research and education programs operated at the DoD I-DREAM4D Consortium, which was recently funded by DoD on a $4 million grant and NSF PREM funded projects. It can also be integrated in the K12 outreach and education efforts organized by the colleges and the consortium at national scale. Results from the research projects supported by this instrument will be disseminated in peer journal articles and national/international conferences to stimulate further understanding and progress of the various research areas of the investigators discussed in this proposal. More importantly, this proposal will:1) Promote a hands-on, entrepreneurial, educational experience, and training of graduate and undergraduate students in advanced materials, nanomaterial design, biomaterials and characterization; 2) Enhance the research infrastructure at UTRGV; 3) Enhance the interdisciplinary research partnership between different departments at UTRGV to better compete for external funding; and 4) Increase the Hispanic Student retention rate at UTRGV

In summary, the Talos™ F200i instrument acquisition will strengthen the existing materials and medical research infrastructure at UTRGV and enhance the research and educational experiences of many students at UTRGV and South Texas region.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Standards/Guidance for Rapid Qualification of Metal-Based Additive Manufacturing
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The American Bureau of Shipping (ABS) is partnering with leading institutions from the DOD-sponsored I-DREAM4D consortium for advanced additive manufacturing and smart manufacturing (University of Texas – Rio Grande Valley [UTRGV], University of Texas – Austin [UTexas], and Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University [VT]) and with the Applied Research Laboratory at Penn State University (ARL PSU) to propose this project for developing Standards/Guidance for Rapid Qualification of Metal-based Additive Manufacturing (AM). The work is focused on equipping the many Technical Authorities, who must ultimately evaluate and approve AM processes and parts for use within various industry segments, to apply best practice qualification methods/tools that can be suitably validated. The term “rapid qualification” indicates our focus on integrating model-based approaches for conducting verification and validation (V&V) activities on AM parts/processes and expert system guidance with reduced traditional physical testing so that Technical Authority qualification can keep up with the growing expansion in the use of AM across many industries. Without development and validation of such standards/guidance, Technical Authority qualification may become a critical path roadblock that will slow the adoption and expansion of AM applications.
The proposed approach leverages unique institutional and personnel capabilities of our co-investigating partners to do the following: (1) Develop a recommended standard/guide for Technical Authorities for implementing best practices in rapid qualification of AM applications, (2) Develop an expert system of recommended guidance on the best uses of AM technologies for different types of applications and associated V&V activities that should be considered for these applications, (3) Develop standard approaches for evaluating and accepting model-based approaches for supporting V&V of AM applications, (4) Develop new best practice model-based approaches for supporting V&V of AM applications, (5) Demonstrate the use of the new standards/guidance for actual AM applications, including demonstration of the standard approach for evaluating and accepting model-based approaches, and (6) Document the recommended standards/guidance in a publication that any Technical Authority may use in setting their own requirements within their industry. CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: In-situ alloying is a highly desired capability by the metal Additive Manufacturing (AM) industry. Research in in-situ alloying could realize the full potential of metal additive manufacturing, supporting material and structure innovation for automobile, energy, and space applications. The preliminary work at University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) demonstrates the possibility of in-situ direct alloying based on elemental metal particles using a Selected Laser Melting AM machine. Despite the low flowability of particles and insufficient diffusion, our work demonstrated the potential of in-situ alloying of configurable binary, ternary, and high entropy alloys (HEAs) directly from multiple elemental metals, using laser and multi-energy sources to control the melting-alloying-solidification cycles involved in the process. However, as with any alloying process, complete diffusion of metal atoms is necessary for the formation of random solid solution, the signature structure of any HEA. In the meantime, the preliminary work at Leibniz Universität Hannover (LUH) reveals that the diffusion of different elements is significantly increased by ultrasound vibration. It is also revealed that, within the vibration environment, metals are melted at a lower temperature than their melting point and grains can be refined. <u>The collaboration between UTRGV and LUH provides a unique opportunity to </u><u>accelerate and control effective diffusion required in processing multi-materials in a single step</u>. In this project, the fundamental mechanisms involved in laser-based in-situ alloying and fusing of multi-elements and multi-materials assisted by ultrasound vibration will be systematically investigated. The team will first investigate the melting, diffusion and solidification of Al-Fe binary systems under ultrasonic vibration, based on a single hatch melt pool. The expected scientific findings include the process behaviors detected using high-speed observations and real-time temperature measurements of laser melt pool. The diffusion behaviors and the resulting material structures across scales will be observed by EDX and XRD. The observed material melting/diffusion/solidification behaviors and resulting material structures created in a single hatch melt pool will allow the team to develop a fundamental process/material behavior relationship considering both laser and ultrasonic process parameters. Multi-hatch strategies will be explored to fabricate samples, which will be studied for mechanical and physical property testing. A process-material-structure property relationship model will then be developed to support future industry adoption of the in-situ alloying based additive processes.

CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The success of the defense industry relies heavily on its innovation capability and its
ability for developing new systems, processes and materials that support innovation needs. While
the challenges facing the defense industry have moved on to a new level in this era, the public
perception of manufacturing remains as not interesting, less rewarding, low tech, dirty and less
secure. This poor perception comes with a lack of interest from young people and a significant gap
of talents needed to drive manufacturing innovation. This proposed project, a joint effort
collaboration of a defense lab, 5 education institutions geographically dispersed across North
America, and 8 defense manufacturers in the U.S. aims to reverse this gap though cultivating an
innovation driven manufacturing education system with instruction covering the total
manufacturing engineering enterprise. The project is designed to attract, engage, train and educate
talent to drive manufacturing and advance manufacturing technologies needed for the future of US
manufacturing and the defense industries.
To accomplish this agenda, a consortium led by the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
(UTRGV) and including, the University of Texas Austin (UT Austin), the University of Texas San
Antonio (UTSA), Virginia State University (Virginia State) and Michigan State University (MSU)
partner with the Army Research Laboratory (ARL) and industry collaborators including the United
Launch Alliance (ULA), Boeing, Ingalls Shipbuilding, Raytheon, StandardAero, Honeywell,
Navistar, and Intrex Aerospace. This geographically distributed team also includes high schools,
typically local to a university, and Career and Technical Education (CTEs) organizations to
provide both secondary and post-secondary activities to generate a pathway system.
Activities that are undertaken to support this pathway include: a research exchange program which
includes student joint supervision with ARL, preparation of Manufacturing Engineers to join and
lead defense industries including development of a defense manufacturing engineering
concentration, a defense and summer research program, a faculty exchange program, a summer
innovation camp for high school students, and student manufacturing exposure programs to assist
with student recruiting. As a result of responding to these multiple goals with corresponding
actions, the consortium team meets the needs of the multiple constituencies that it serves. Students
have a pathway from high school to an assignment in advanced manufacturing for defense
industries, and the industries have a direct opportunity to attract and hire qualified technical talent.
Our proposal focuses on Innovative Advanced Manufacturing and specifically on Systems and
Materials, and Additive Manufacturing Technologies which are capable of producing lightweight
structures and materials. This tightly targeted approach has been encouraged by ARL, our military
laboratory partner, and the defense industry partners in our consortium: Boeing, Raytheon,

CONGRANT.TITLE: GOALI: Study of Selective Laser Alloying of Elemental Metal Powders
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Overview:
Selective laser alloying, an innovative process first attempted at PIs? lab, showed potential of advancing
the scientific and engineering foundations in material processing. In this novel approach, instead of prealloyed
powders, pure elemental powders are selectively melted by a laser beam, and then react into
desired alloys at desired locations. This creates unique opportunities to transform
material/structure/device design and fabrication with following advantages: 1) free forming with
adjustable material composition/property along all three axes. 2) significantly reduced energy
consumption in 3D laser processing utilizing energy released from the reaction process, 3) 3D forming of
high melting point ceramic materials from elemental powders at much lower processing temperature, 4)
creating micron-scale porous structures with controllable shape, size, and desired 3-dimensional spatial
arrangements.
While the concept of this process was successfully proved with patents pending by a team of students and
faculty at PIs? lab (US Patent 6493-03100), our initial investigation also exposed fundamental research
questions that must be addressed before it can spin off innovations in a stream of applications in both
commercial and defense sectors. Targeted on these challenges/opportunities, an interdisciplinary team of
experts from equipment manufacturers, application user (ARL), and academic researchers, will jointly
investigate the important research questions aiming to understand the structure-property-processing
relationships associated with the novel process. Specifically, the team will investigate the intrinsic
heating-prereaction-alloying-melting-solidification process cycle at multi-spatial-temporal scales, so as to
predict process behavior and property of the micro/meso/macro structures created. Special phenomena
such as the speculated Kirkendall effect, Kirkendall porosity, and exothermic reaction between elemental
powders at microscale will be investigated. PIs will also develop heat models to direct the experiments,
eventually help better understanding of the structure-property-processing relationships, control of the
process, and attaining desired structures and properties of fabricated products.
Intellectual Merit:
Currently, metal free-forming utilizing exothermic reaction between elemental powders has not been well
addressed and studied in literature. Study of Kirkendall effects in a powder based binary system at micro
scale can be another important contribution to the literature. The study will also advance knowledge
about pore formation in the select laser alloying which can help understand the determining factors for
the size, shape, and 3 dimensional spatial arrangement of the pore networks. This can eventually help the
team to develop the process-property relationship for this novel process and for wider adoption in
industry. Knowledge discovered in this research can be applied to processing of other multi-material
metal powder systems.
Broader Impacts:
If succeeds, this research can spin off innovations in a stream of applications that require extremely hard
materials with extremely high melting temperature, excellent heat conductivity, oxidation stability,
resistance to mechanical erosion, and good electrical conductivity. This research could also create a
transformative technology to significantly reduce energy consumption in laser processing and enable the
fabrication of porous structured materials integrating with 3D free forming for applications in defense,
medical, aerospace and oil industries. The research projects will provide exciting education and research
opportunities for the graduate and undergraduate students at UTRGV. UTRGV is a major Hispanic
serving institution; around 90% of its 30,000 enrolled students are Hispanic Americans. The team also
has strong record in technology transfer and commercialization. Dr. Li and Xu are now participating in
the NSF I-Corp program. Technologies develop in this research project will be eventually transferred or
commercialized to benefit the communities and society at the regional and national levels.

The Thermoacoustic Atmospheric Water Generator (TAAWG) can condense water vapor on the surface of its regenerator (porous media), therefore it can provide a reliable and easily-accessible water supply to people under aforementioned conditions. CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The significant growth of population, deteriorating environment and climate change have led to increased need for freshwater. Nevertheless, water is still limited resource to most of arid and rural areas, it can also be considered scarce in urban areas when natural disasters happen (e.g. hurricane or earthquake). The Thermoacoustic Atmospheric Water Generator (TAAWG) can condense water vapor on the surface of its regenerator (porous media), therefore it can provide a reliable and easily-accessible water supply to people under aforementioned conditions. However, due to the complicated transport phenomenon involved, the multiphase oscillating flow and heat transfer in porous media remain poorly understood and analytically intractable. INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>Concentrated solar power (CSP) is a reliable renewable energy source that is progressively lowering its cost of energy. However, the heat loss due to reflected and emitted radiation hinders the maximum achievable thermal efficiency for solar receiver tubes on the solar tower. Current solar selective coatings cannot withstand the high temperatures that come with state-of-the-art CSP towers often needing to be recoated soon after initial operation. We intend to use Inconel 718 with different additive manufacturing (AM) practices to construct surfaces that allow for more light-trapping to occur. By adjusting printing parameters, we can tailor a surface to allow for more absorption while diminishing emitted radiation heat loss. By using COMSOL Multiphysics, we can generate these theoretical surfaces to emulate a printed surface, and using the coupled Multiphysics we can simulate how the surface dictates radiation properties. Our results show that by having a rougher surface we can enhance the absorptivity of Inconel 718 (IN718) by 38.8%. We expect this work to transform how solar absorber tubes are manufactured without using selective coatings and supplement the US Department of Energy (DOE) 2030 SunShot Initiative.</jats:p>

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Experimental investigation of various energy-absorbing layer materials and sodium alginate viscosities on the jet formation in laser-induced-forward-transfer (LIFT) bioprinting
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: <jats:p>Laser-induced-forward-transfer (LIFT) bioprinting technology has been viewed as a regenerative medicine technology because of its high printing quality and good cell viability. To stabilize the jet to achieve high-quality printing, an energy-absorbing layer (EAL) can be introduced. In this study, three materials (graphene, gelatin, and gold) were utilized as the EAL. The effect of each EAL on the jet generation process was investigated. Besides, the effect of graphene EAL thickness was addressed for various experimental conditions. The jet generation process using sodium alginate solutions with different concentrations (1 and 2 wt. %) was also discussed to investigate the effect of viscosity. The time sequence images of the formed jets utilizing three EALs showed that both graphene EAL and gelatin EAL can promote the formation of jet flow. For the gold EAL, no jet flow was observed. This study provides experimental verifications that the interaction between laser and EAL materials can result in different jets due to various dominant interaction mechanisms. For example, strong absorption in the infrared range for the graphene EAL, strong scattering loss for the gelatin EAL, and strong absorption in the ultraviolet range but weak absorption in the infrared for the gold EAL. We also observed the holes left on the EAL after the printing was completed. The thermal effect is dominant to create regular and round shape holes for the graphene EAL, but it changes to the mechanical effect for the gold EAL because of the existence of irregular and unorganized holes. In addition, we identified the existence of an input laser energy threshold value for a certain thickness graphene EAL. More laser energy is required to break down thicker graphene EALs, which will result in a higher initial jet velocity. Furthermore, we explored the effect of sodium alginate (SA) solution's viscosity on the generated jet. We found that a high-viscosity SA solution can result in a low initial jet velocity, a short jet, and small droplets on the receiving substrate. The findings from this study help determine the mechanisms of EAL–laser interaction with different EAL materials in the LIFT process. This work aims to facilitate the development of new EAL and bioink to achieve stable jet formation and high printing quality in future LIFT bioprinting.</jats:p>

               <jats:p>Laser induced forward transfer (LIFT) bioprinting has been viewed as a new and actively developed three-dimensional bioprinting technology due to its high accuracy and good cell viability. The printing quality is highly dependent on the jet formation and its stability in the LIFT bioprinting process. The objective of this study is to investigate the effect of a graphene Energy Absorbing Layer (EAL) and alginate hydrogel (SA) (w.t. 1% and 2%) viscosity on jet generation in the LIFT bioprinting process. Since SA exhibits a shear-thinning behavior, it is a non-Newtonian fluid. The effect of EAL thickness and SA’s viscosity were addressed for various experimental conditions. After the laser irradiated on the quartz substrate, small holes caused by laser interaction appeared in the interaction area on the EAL. The EAL substrate with multiple holes was examined using an optical microscope, and the morphology of holes was observed and compared. The images of jet generation showed that graphene EAL can assist in the transfer of SA with a low laser energy absorption rate. The viscosity of the SA also plays a significant role in the generation of a stable jet for SA transfer. For the cases with the same laser energy input, the jet generated using higher viscosity bioink had a smaller initial velocity, which eventually led to a shorter jet length. The findings in this study will facilitate the development of new EAL in LIFT bioprinting.</jats:p>

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>The powder bed fusion (PBF) process is widely adopted in many manufacturing industries because of its capability to 3D print complex parts with micro-scale precision. In PBF process, a thermal energy source is used to selectively fuse powder particles layer by layer to build a part. The build quality in the PBF process primarily depends on the thermal energy deposition and properties of the powder bed. Powder flowability, powder spreading, and packing fraction are key factors that determine the properties of a powder bed. Therefore, the study of these process parameters is essential to better understand the PBF process. In our study, we developed a two-dimensional powder bed model using the granular package of the LAMMPS molecular dynamics simulator. Cloud-based deposition was adopted for pouring powder particles on the powder bed. The spreading of particles over the substrate was mimicked like a powder bed system. The powder flowability in the proposed study was analyzed by varying the particle size distribution. The simulation results showed that a greater number of larger particles in a power sample results in an increase in the Angle of Repose (AOR) which ultimately affects the flowability. Two different kinds of recoater geometry were considered in this study: circular and rectangular blades. Simulation results showed that depending on the recoater shape there is a change in the packing fraction in the powder bed. Cross-sectional analysis of the power bed showed a significant presence of voids when a greater number of larger particles existed in the powder batch. The packing fraction of the powder bed was found to be a strong function of particle size distribution. These analyses help understand the influence of particle size and recoater shape on the powder bed properties. Findings from this study help to provide a guideline for choosing particle size distribution if the spherical particles are considered. While the present study focuses on the spherical powder particles, the proposed system can also be adapted to the study of powder bed with aspherical particles.</jats:p>

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Ultrafast Laser Direct Writing of Conductive Patterns on Polyimide Substrate
INTELLCONT.TITLE_SECONDARY: Volume 1: Additive Manufacturing; Biomanufacturing; Life Cycle Engineering; Manufacturing Equipment and Automation; Nano/Micro/Meso Manufacturing
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>Laser direct writing (LDW) is a fast and cost-effective method for printing conductive patterns in flexible polymer substrates. The electrical, chemical, and mechanical properties of polyimide (PI) make it an attractive material choice for laser writing of conductive circuits in such polymer. Electrically insulating PI has shown great potential for flexible printed electronics as LDW enables selective carbonization in the bulk of such material leading to the formation of conductive lines. However, existing studies in this area reveal a few key limitations of this approach including limited conductivity of written structures and fragility of carbonized PI. Therefore, more research is required to overcome those limitations and reap the benefits of the LDW approach in writing flexible electronic circuits in PI. The proposed study investigates potential approaches to enhance the electrical conductivity of femtosecond laser written bulk carbon structures in PI films. Deposition of laser energy was varied by changing key process parameters such as pulse energy, pulse picker divider, and hatch distance of laser scan to maximize the conductively of the carbon structure. The experimental findings show a strong dependency of laser energy deposition on the conductivity carbon structures in PI films. To further enhance the electrical conductivity of laser written structures, the feasibility of adding copper microparticles to the PI solution and subsequent laser carbonization was studied. The proposed LDW of conductive lines has potential in flexible electronic circuits and sensing applications.</jats:p>

China University of Mining and Technology

INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: International Communication of Heat and Mass Transfer
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: The evaporation of brine droplet has critical impacts on the zero-liquid-discharge thermal desalination process. A good understanding of the evaporation of brine droplets provides guidelines for the design of thermal desalination system, and offers insights for applications when solvent droplet evaporation process is involved. In this study, brine droplets with different salt mass concentrations were placed in a chamber with controlled temperature and relative humidity. The evaporation and crystallization processes were then visualized through a high speed camera by employing the pendant droplet method. The results showed that the evaporation rate increases with the decrease of relative humidity, the increase of temperature, and the decrease of salt mass concentration. After the evaporation was finished, we can observe that the crystal grew along the filament during the evaporation and remained on it. A salt shell was formed at the outside, while the droplet still contained some amount of brine inside when the evaporation rate was low. Consequently, the evaporation mechanism was changed once the salt shell was formed, the water molecules needed to overcome the pressure difference inside and outside the salt shell, and diffused through the shell for further evaporation. A multi-variable fitted quadratic regression model was developed with R2=0.974 to describe the relationship among the evaporation rate, mass concentration, relative humidity and temperature. Because the regression model was based on experimental data with temperature varying from 30ºC to 60ºC, a predicted result of brine droplet’s evaporation rate with various mass concentrations under 75°C and 0% RH showed a good agreement with the experiment data, therefore the developed regression model can be extended for high temperature (<100ºC, no boiling) applications.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Zinc ferrite based gas sensors: A review
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Flammable, explosive and toxic gases, such as hydrogen, hydrogen sulfide and volatile organic compounds vapor, are major threats to the ecological environment safety and human health. Among the available technologies, gas sensing is a vital component, and has been widely studied in literature for early detection and warning. As a metal oxide semiconductor, zinc ferrite (ZnFe2O4) represents a kind of promising gas sensing material with a spinel structure, which also shows a fine gas sensing performance to reducing gases. Due to its great potentials and widespread applications, this article is intended to provide a review on the latest development in zinc ferrite based gas sensors. We first discuss the general gas sensing mechanism of ZnFe2O4 sensor. This is followed by a review of the recent progress about zinc ferrite based gas sensors from several aspects: different micro-morphology, element doping and heterostructure materials. In the end, we propose that combining ZnFe2O4 which provides unique microstructure (such as the multi-layer porous shells hollow structure), with the semiconductors such as graphene, which provide excellent physical properties. It is expected that the mentioned composites contribute to improving selectivity, long-term stability, and other sensing performance of sensors at room or low temperature.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Selective Laser Melting of Mechanically Alloyed Metastable Al5Fe2 Powders
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: ASME Journal of Manufacturing Science and Engineering
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Aluminum alloys, which are high-strength lightweight materials, were processed by selective laser melting (SLM) with high-energy consumption and poor finish due to quick heat dissipation. Previous investigations reported that SLM with 300 W laser power and 500 mm/s scanning speed can process the aluminum alloys, such as Al-Si12 and AlSi10Mg. This work aims to process the powders to alter their properties and to reduce the laser intensity required in the process, and it also reports that the SLM-processed Al–Fe alloys utilize the metastable alloy by mechanical alloying (MA). The elemental Al and Fe powders were first alloyed in a ball mill in a relative short time period (∼15 h) employing high milling intensities, high ball-to-powder ratio (≥20:1), and high milling velocities (≥400 rpm), which produced fine metastable Al–Fe powders, and these powders were processed later by the SLM. The optimum laser power, the scanning speed, hatch distance, and substrate temperature were investigated by a series of experiments. Experimental results indicated that decreasing the laser energy density while increasing the laser scanning speed can benefit for smoother laser hatch lines, and the metastable Al5Fe2 alloy powders can be processed and stabilized under a 200-W laser energy density and a scanning speed of 1000 mm/s. It is expected that the combination of pre-excited materials in a metastable phase will open a new window to optimize the SLM process for aluminum alloys and other metallic alloys.

INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: Institute of Industrial and Systems Engineers
INTELLCONT.EDITORS: K. Barker, D. Berry, and C. Rainwater
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: According to the Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC), wind energy systems are becoming prevalent and economically accessible for small-town municipalities. With most municipalities depending on hydroelectric and fossils fuels, the question is what fraction of their electrical source, wind energy can provide while being economically advantageous. The Brownsville Public Utilities Board (BPUB) serves 730 miles in South Texas and is looking for alternative systems with inexpensive levelized cost. This research will assess wind system as an alternative due to its low cost of energy production. To determine how wind system has a long-lasting service, several elements of the wind system are evaluated. In addition, a case study is presented based on BPUB’S electrical production system and expected growth. From these values and using the LCEO calculator, the value of LCOE was found as $62.27 per MWH. Since the objective was to increase the power output by 25MW, the new plant size was 125MW. The effects of this change did not affect the value of LCOE significantly. Therefore, the change was seen to be feasible.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Selective laser alloying of elemental titanium and boron powder: thermal models and experimental validation
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: The purpose of this article was to introduce the concept of selective laser alloying (SLA) to print 3D parts directly from elemental powders, and report findings on an investigation of the governing thermal models of the process. Considering the effects of exothermic reaction between Ti and B during the alloying process, thermal models with three group of parameters were developed to predict the phenomena induced in the selective laser alloying process. To validate these models, a series of experiments, with different molar ratios between Ti and B, were conducted on Renishaw AM250 using premixed elemental Ti and B powders. The experiments validated the SLA concept and the results matched consistently with the models’ predictions, which validated the models.

PRESENT.ABSTRACT: Cold Spray is a type of thermal metal spraying which uses heated gas/air to propel metal powder onto the surface of a substrate to create a coating or repair damaged or corroded metal components. The powder feedstock materials are spherical gas atomized metal powders ranging in size from 20-50 microns in diameter for best results. Cold spray systems use low temperatures ranging from 200-900 °C compared to existing additive manufacturing methods which use much higher temperatures to melt metal. These lower heating temperatures only semi-melt the metal powder particles allowing for them to undergo plastic deformation as they are deposited onto the surface of the substrate. The main objective of this project is to develop and characterize cold spray coatings using aluminum, copper, and nickel powders deposited on different substrates varying processing parameters. As cold spray can be used in different coating applications with a wide range of different metals and alloys, coatings have an unlimited range in applications where rapid repair and high-quality coatings are needed. The ease of use of this technology has a promising future in aerospace and defense applications as it provides a low-cost solution in corrosion prevention and repair of damaged components.

The experiments validated the SLA concept and the results matched consistently with the models’ predictions, which validated the models.
